title: Foreknowledge presupposes settled future truth
explanation: On the stipulated definitions, infallible prior knowledge that a future action will occur requires that the corresponding proposition be true prior to the act.
caveat: A temporalist may revise the account of ‘prior’; an atemporalist may replace foreknowledge with timeless knowledge.
objections: Reject the temporal formulation of divine knowledge.
Argue that knowledge can track a future truth without its being presently truth-valued.

assessment.framework: Classical reasoning over the stated definitions; no automated modal or temporal proof.
assessment.scope: Same divine subject, domain and sense of the relevant temporal/modal terms. Hybrid readings require reformulation.
assessment.justification: Retained only under the temporal, factive reading of foreknowledge and the same domain of future free-action propositions. Present truth is not causal necessity.

title: Open and settled future
explanation: The two claims explicitly quantify over the same class of future free-action propositions and respectively deny and affirm universal present bivalence.
caveat: The conflict disappears if the claims concern different propositions, times, or senses of determinacy.

assessment.framework: Classical reasoning over the stated definitions; no automated modal or temporal proof.
assessment.scope: Same divine subject, domain and sense of the relevant temporal/modal terms. Hybrid readings require reformulation.
assessment.justification: Universal bivalence and its existential denial concern the same propositions and prior assessment time. No general theorem about future semantics is asserted.

title: Timelessness and temporal succession
explanation: Under the definitions used here, one claim denies and the other affirms that God undergoes temporal succession.
caveat: Hybrid views may distinguish phases or senses of temporality; they should not affirm both claims without qualification.
objections: Adopt timelessness sans creation and temporality with creation.
Distinguish metaphysical time from another ordering relation.

assessment.framework: Classical reasoning over the stated definitions; no automated modal or temporal proof.
assessment.scope: Same divine subject, domain and sense of the relevant temporal/modal terms. Hybrid readings require reformulation.
assessment.justification: Conceptual exclusion under the unqualified same-subject definitions. Hybrid phases require different claims and cannot be represented by this pair.

title: Libertarian freedom and determination
explanation: The two claims are incompatible if divine determination is causal determination by the prior conditions excluded by LIBERTARIAN. A timeless decree needs a further account of this relation.
caveat: A compatibilist can retain freedom but not freedom in the stipulated libertarian sense.
objections: Restrict divine determination so that some actions remain undetermined.
Adopt a compatibilist analysis of freedom.

assessment.framework: Classical reasoning over the stated definitions; no automated modal or temporal proof.
assessment.scope: Same divine subject, domain and sense of the relevant temporal/modal terms. Hybrid readings require reformulation.
assessment.justification: Downgraded: prior-condition determination and a possibly timeless decree are not automatically the same relation. The temporal/causal bridge remains unresolved.

title: Theological fatalist argument
explanation: If God’s past belief is fixed and infallibly entails the later act, transfer of accidental necessity appears to make the act unavoidable; PAP then places pressure on libertarian freedom.
caveat: This is not encoded as a deduction. Ockhamists dispute that the relevant past belief is a hard fact; others reject transfer, PAP, or the temporal framing.
objections: Treat the past belief as a soft fact partly about the future.
Reject the relevant transfer principle.
Ground freedom in sourcehood rather than alternative possibilities.
Adopt timeless rather than prior divine knowledge.

assessment.framework: Classical reasoning over the stated definitions; no automated modal or temporal proof.
assessment.scope: Same divine subject, domain and sense of the relevant temporal/modal terms. Hybrid readings require reformulation.
assessment.justification: Retained as a dialectical outline. The general past-fixity sentence does not supply the hard-fact premise or the full necessity-to-inability bridge.

title: Timeless knowledge described as prior
explanation: The definition of foreknowledge used here locates divine knowledge prior to events, while timelessness denies temporal location. A timeless knower may know future-to-us events, but not literally beforehand.
caveat: This is largely terminological if ‘foreknowledge’ is used loosely for knowledge of what creatures call the future.
objections: Replace FOREKNOWLEDGE with an atemporal knowledge claim.
Use ‘future’ relationally to creaturely time without temporally locating God.

assessment.framework: Classical reasoning over the stated definitions; no automated modal or temporal proof.
assessment.scope: Same divine subject, domain and sense of the relevant temporal/modal terms. Hybrid readings require reformulation.
assessment.justification: Retained as interpretive pressure: a temporal reading conflicts with timelessness, but a relational or loose reading changes the proposition.

title: Succession and intrinsic changelessness
explanation: Temporally ordered divine states appear to involve intrinsic change, while strong immutability denies it.
caveat: Mere temporal endurance need not entail intrinsic change; the pressure concerns the stronger claim that God has successively different intrinsic states.
objections: Hold that only God’s extrinsic relations change.
Distinguish temporal location from qualitative change.

assessment.framework: Classical reasoning over the stated definitions; no automated modal or temporal proof.
assessment.scope: Same divine subject, domain and sense of the relevant temporal/modal terms. Hybrid readings require reformulation.
assessment.justification: Retained as interpretive pressure. Temporally ordered states do not alone establish intrinsically different states.

title: Creative freedom’s alternatives
explanation: If God’s actual creative choice is free and such freedom requires an alternative, then a relevant alternative to this total creative choice must be possible.
caveat: This conclusion uses the broad alternative encoded in CONTINGENT-CREATION; finer-grained alternatives may require a more specific claim.
objections: Reject alternative possibilities as necessary for divine freedom.
Argue that only alternatives within creation, not non-creation of this total order, are required.

assessment.framework: Classical reasoning over the stated definitions; no automated modal or temporal proof.
assessment.scope: Same divine subject, domain and sense of the relevant temporal/modal terms. Hybrid readings require reformulation.
assessment.justification: Added CREATION-ALTERNATIVE: alternatives in choice must involve omitting or replacing this total created order, not merely different intentions with identical effects.

title: Simplicity and contingent effects
explanation: Critics argue that if God’s willing is identical with God’s necessary, simple being, it is difficult to explain how that willing has a contingent total effect rather than a necessary one.
caveat: This is a modal-collapse objection, not a formal consequence of simplicity alone. Classical replies distinguish necessary divine willing from contingent relations or effects.
objections: Distinguish God’s intrinsic act from its contingent extrinsic terminus.
Deny that a necessary cause must have its effect necessarily.
Use an account of Cambridge properties or contingent relations.

assessment.framework: Classical reasoning over the stated definitions; no automated modal or temporal proof.
assessment.scope: Same divine subject, domain and sense of the relevant temporal/modal terms. Hybrid readings require reformulation.
assessment.justification: Added necessary existence to the triggering cluster. Identity of willing, necessity of its content, and transfer to effects are still disputed; this remains an objection outline, never a deduction.

title: Middle knowledge and possible libertarian agency
explanation: The Molinist reading presupposes possible libertarian creaturely agency. Denying that possibility challenges this reading of middle knowledge; it does not establish that any actual human acts freely.
caveat: Knowing conditionals about free choices alone does not establish possible antecedents or actual free actions.
objections: Counterfactuals may have impossible or unactualized antecedents.
Clarify whether the claim asserts possible free agency or merely knowledge of conditionals.

assessment.framework: Classical reasoning over the stated definitions; no automated modal or temporal proof.
assessment.scope: Same divine subject, domain and sense of the relevant temporal/modal terms. Hybrid readings require reformulation.
assessment.justification: Removed the actual-action conclusion. Possible libertarian subject matter is an interpretive assumption of the Molinist reading, not a consequence of knowing arbitrary counterfactuals. Downgraded to an explicit interpretive tension when possibility is denied.

title: Nonresistant nonbelief and a perfectly loving God
explanation: Write G for LOVING-GOD and N for NONRESISTANT-NONBELIEF. The selected bridge is G → ¬N. Together with N it entails ¬G by modus tollens. The deduction does not establish the truth of either premise.
caveat: This is an editorial propositional reconstruction, not the full modal argument. It targets only the specified perfectly loving personal God. Denying or suspending a premise does not establish that God exists.
objections: The bridge may fail if perfect love permits temporary nonbelief for sufficient reasons.
Whether nonresistant nonbelief occurs, and how capacity and resistance are understood, are disputed.
Rejecting the target conception changes the subject; it is not a refutation of all religious conceptions.

assessment.scope: G means the specified perfectly loving personal God; N uses the same finite persons, capacities and times in both premises.
assessment.justification: All four valuations of G and N are checked against the encoded formula in the test suite. This checks form, not soundness or fidelity to the full modal argument.

objectionTargets.text: Dispute whether perfect love excludes every relevant episode of nonbelief.
Assess the existential premise without assigning motives to individual users.
